title: University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight On
content:
Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. U of M now calls the project a “research computing center” and, if all goes to its plan, construction will begin on a 125,000 square foot facility in late 2027. The data center could expand to “no more than 300,000 square feet,” according to a U of M blog post.

During the regent’s meeting, faculty, staff, and members of the community shared their thoughts on the data center’s construction.

title: Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You’ll Be the Main Character
content:
Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized “shows” starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.

Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don’t end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called “creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user,” describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called “My Channel,” which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make “the user as the protagonist for the whole video.” The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.

title: “I’m not going to remove the repository”
content:
There is a hacking tool called ARTEX that is causing havoc around the world. It lets a hacker plug in their LLM of choice, and ARTEX will then spin up a bunch of AI subagents focused on different aspects of hacking, such as scoping out a target or stealing data. This tool can complete an entire hack of a target in just a few hours. The original author of ARTEX took down the tool in October after it became clear that bad people were using it. But, as I write below, ARTEX is free. Several people are still distributing it on GitHub. I spoke to them about it, asked them why, and for their thoughts about requests to take the tool down. 

And as I’m writing this, NVIDIA just said it has reinstated Jensen Huang as President, CEO, and Board Director. Hahahahahahahahahha.

title: ‘The Code Is Already Copied Everywhere’: The AI Hacking Tool Causing Havoc Around the World
content: ARTEX, an open source framework that makes it easy for AI agents to hack companies at superspeed, is causing havoc. People using the tool appear to include Chinese hackers breaking into targets for espionage, and financially-motivated hackers too. Earlier this month, the FBI published a warning to potential targets, and said hackers using ARTEX have targeted government, healthcare, telecommunications, legal, defense, financial services, and semiconductor sectors globally.

title: Scientists Discover New and Horrible Eagle-Based Way Our Ancestors Died
content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! Here are the studies this week that dive-bombed our ancestors, brightened the sky, recalled an old tune, and got hosed by marine mucus.

First, scientists discover that eagles are hunting large baboons, hinting that early human relatives once sated ancient avian appetites. Then: star-on-star contact, a musical memory lane, and the secrets of cetacean snot. 

As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.

Hobaiter, Catherine et al. “Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate.” American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

Death came from the sky for early humans, according to a new study that suggests giant eagles preyed on our ancestors far more recently than was previously known.

title: Behind the Blog: Keeping It Together
content:
This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss hippo physiology, Shenmue, and tricky interviews.

SAM: All anyone is talking about this week is GTA VI and a famous hippo, two things I have relatively passing interest in. GTA looks sick but I am very busy playing my interpersonal chores game of choice, Spiritfarer, in 20 minute increments three nights a week max, so I’ll be doing that for a while. 

The hippo situation is honestly very crazy to me (and sad ofc), a merely casual Fiona appreciator. But I'm finding the meta-discourse around the hippo situation more interesting than what actually happened; it seems like a ton of people have become parenting experts, hippo surgery experts, knit hat aerodynamics experts, and zoo enclosure design experts in the span of a week. In some cases it has gotten nasty. I think the situation so perfectly encapsulates the toxicity of online discourse, professors will probably teach it in mass media classes by next semester.

content:

The company, run by defendant Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar and an unnamed business associate, began in 2020 and claimed to offer data recovery services for victims of ransomware.

title: High-End Furniture Marketplace AptDeco Is Taking People’s Furniture and Not Paying Them
content:
This article has been updated with comment from AptDeco.

Last month, Erin sold a $3,000 large designer table on AptDeco, a white glove high-end furniture marketplace. More than a month later, she feels like she’s been literally robbed.

“AptDeco sent three men to physically collect my table on October 13, and here we are on November 16, with no payment and no concrete explanation for where my $2,000 (after their absurd $900 fee) is,” Erin told me. “It genuinely feels like I’ve had something stolen from me.”

AptDeco is a Y Combinator-backed company whose entire purpose is to take the risk out of places like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist for designer furniture resale. It advertises itself as “simple and seamless,” and says “we handle pickup, delivery, and payments,” and claims that it pays sellers “within 5-10 business days.” But over the last few months, people who have sold furniture on the platform say that AptDeco has sold their furniture and taken it from their houses, but hasn’t paid them. 404 Media agreed to only use Erin’s first name because she is still trying to get her money from the company.

title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
content:
Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.

According to the study, “Redlining in the Age of AI: The Relationship between Data Center Locations and Race in the US” majority-Black neighborhoods have 2.2 times the odds of hosting a data center than a white neighborhood in the same state. The number goes up to 2.6 in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods and 4.2 times in majority-Asian neighborhoods. “As the share of Black, Hispanic, and Asian residents in a neighborhood increases, so do the odds that the neighborhood hosts a data center,” the researchers wrote.

title: ICE Is Paying AT&T to Dig Through a Mountain of Call Records
content:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts have called it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data. 

The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning non-customers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.

title: Charting American Culture in News Footage of ‘Grand Theft Auto’
content:
Some people spent the week leading up to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI replaying the old games. I, sicko that I am, spent it watching TV news coverage of the franchise from the past 20 years.

Grand Theft Auto has been a staple of cable and broadcast TV news since at least the release of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001. I’ve been an adult for all of it; I’ve had a front row seat for two decades of moral panics, parental freakouts, and bizarre political theater. The games and the broader culture’s reaction to them have changed dramatically in that time. In 2001, newscasters worried GTA III was training an army of young men to kill. In 2026, The New York Times earnestly quoted Bell Hooks in its review of GTA VI.

For mainstream news, GTA is the ur-video game. The open world that mirrors our own, the prevalence of sex and death, and the increasingly realistic simulations and graphics pointed towards the dream of what a video game could be. GTA is the American id made manifest.

title: Massive New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
content:
A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

Gallup’s study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.
